claims.text: Equimolar or near-equimolar CoCrFeNiTi can exist as a homogeneous single-phase solid solution.
The initial single-phase CoCrFeNiTi solid solution has low lattice distortion.
Single-phase near-equimolar CoCrFeNiTi has relatively low hardness and strength.
Single-phase near-equimolar CoCrFeNiTi has high plasticity and favorable machinability.
A homogeneous lattice in this alloy favors easy dislocation glide.
Favorable dislocation glide promotes rapid dynamic recovery during deformation.
Dynamic recovery in this alloy proceeds through dislocation climb and annihilation.
Rapid dynamic recovery prevents substantial accumulation of dislocations.
Limited dislocation accumulation restricts strain hardening and thereby limits hardness and strength.
Dislocation density and subgrain or cell structures are governed by the balance between deformation-induced dislocation generation and recovery-induced annihilation.
Cryogenic deformation suppresses dynamic-recovery kinetics relative to room-temperature deformation.
At room temperature, deformation will produce high plasticity with only a small increase in dislocation density.
At room temperature, deformation will cause only a modest increase in hardness and strength.
Cryogenic deformation will cause a steeper increase in dislocation density than room-temperature deformation.
Cryogenic deformation will produce greater strain hardening, hardness, and strength than room-temperature deformation.
The proposed mechanism applies only while near-equimolar CoCrFeNiTi remains a single-phase solid solution without precipitates or phase separation.
Precipitate formation, phase separation, or extreme loading rates and temperatures may alter the governing recovery kinetics.

contradictions.description: Cryogenic loading is a central controlled condition used to test the predicted mechanism, but the boundary says the hypothesis is limited to loading conditions typical of room-temperature deformation and may not hold at extreme temperatures. The applicability of the mechanistic prediction to the cryogenic arm is therefore ambiguous.
